title: Calcium Deficiency in Plants: Signs, Causes and How to Fix It
metaTitle: Calcium Deficiency in Plants: Signs and Fixes
metaDescription: Calcium deficiency shows on the young leaves first. See the signs crop by crop, what causes it, and the fertilizer sold here that fixes it.
excerpt: Calcium deficiency in plants starts on the young leaves and the growing tip. Calcium builds the walls of new cells and holds the cell membranes together. So growing tips, young leaves, roots and fruit need a steady supply. It also activates enzymes and supports normal root growth. Peanut needs it to form seed in the pods. Here are the signs in each crop, what brings it, how to be sure and the fertilizer that fixes it.

heroImage.alt: Tomatoes with dark sunken rot at the blossom end: the classic calcium shortage sign in fruit

blocks.text: Calcium does not move out of old leaves. It travels only with the water that the roots pull up to the leaves. So the damage shows on the growing tips, young leaves and fruit, which the water stream reaches last.
Calcium deficiency symptoms

Growing tips of shoots and roots turn brown and die. New leaves come out cupped, crinkled or stuck together at the edges. In corn the new leaves fail to unfold, and in rice the tips of the youngest leaves turn white and roll. Tomato, pepper and eggplant show blossom end rot, a dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom of the fruit. Buds and blossoms may also fall early.
Calcium deficiency by crop

Each crop shows it its own way. So find yours in the tables below, then open its page for the photo and the full fix, like the one for [calcium in rice](/nutrient-deficiencies/rice-nutrient-deficiency#calcium).

blocks.text: What causes calcium deficiency

Strongly acid, leached upland soils and coarse sandy soils hold little calcium, and soils from serpentine rock are poor in it too. In fruit, the usual cause is uneven watering, drought or root damage, which keeps calcium from reaching the fruit even when the soil has enough. Heavy nitrogen, ammonium fertilizers and big potash doses also cut calcium uptake. On very acid soils, the acidity itself often stunts the roots before any calcium signs appear.
How to be sure it is calcium

Boron shortage also kills the growing tip and deforms young leaves, and herbicide injury can stop new corn leaves from unfolding. Blossom end rot is not a disease, so it never spreads from plant to plant the way a fruit rot does. Test the soil pH and exchangeable calcium at a DA Regional Soils Laboratory, because most calcium trouble comes with acid soil. A leaf tissue test helps, but it cannot show if enough calcium reaches the fruit, so check the watering record too.
How to fix calcium deficiency

On acid soils, apply agricultural lime or dolomite by the soil test, because it raises the pH and adds calcium. Where the pH is already right or the crop needs an acid soil, gypsum or superphosphate (0 20 0) adds calcium. For blossom end rot, keep the soil evenly moist with mulch and regular watering, and go easy on ammonium fertilizers.

A calcium nitrate spray at about 800 grams per 100 liters of water is a typical rate in a Haifa vegetable guide. It can slow the damage on the parts it wets, but even watering does more for blossom end rot.

How to keep calcium deficiency away

Lime acid fields by the soil test and keep the pH where the crop likes it. Water fruit crops evenly, mulch to hold moisture, and avoid heavy nitrogen and ammonium fertilizer while the fruit is forming.

blocks.title: Too much is a problem too
blocks.text: Too much lime pushes the pH up and locks up iron, zinc, manganese and boron. Over liming, mostly on sandy soils, can bring on zinc and iron shortage.

blocks.text: Calcium deficiency questions

items.q: What does calcium deficiency look like?
items.a: The growing tips and youngest leaves suffer first, turning brown, cupped or stuck together, and the roots stop growing. In tomato, pepper and eggplant it shows as blossom end rot on the fruit.

items.q: What causes blossom end rot in tomatoes?
items.a: It is a calcium shortage inside the fruit, usually caused by uneven watering or drought, not by a lack of calcium in the soil. Keep the soil evenly moist, mulch, and avoid too much nitrogen.

items.q: What is the best fertilizer for calcium deficiency?
items.a: On acid soils, agricultural lime or dolomite applied by the soil test is the usual source. Where the pH is already right, use gypsum, and calcium nitrate works as a spray.

items.q: Will spraying calcium fix blossom end rot?
items.a: A calcium spray can slow it on the fruit it wets, but it rarely cures it. Even watering and mulch fix the cause, since calcium reaches the fruit only with the water the plant takes up.
